articleTitle: Fixation of atmospheric nitrogen by electricity
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: When bringing forward this paper I intended to draw the attention of the local electrical engineers to the great field they had before them in South Africa for applying their knowledge and forces. I did not think, however, that much discussion would arise out of it, as this industry is unknown as yet in South Africa, and probably very few had any practical knowledge of it. In my opinion, it is not men who create an industry, but an industry that creates men. As soon as the rulers of the Union realise what riches are hidden in the first ten inches of the soil of South Africa, and as soon as South African agricultural products appear on the European markets—to conquer them—the manufacture of artificial nitrogen must and will spring up locally, and the new industry will then create those electrical engineers who will take a keen interest in this question. I hope in five or ten years time my paper will be more commented upon and discussed than it has been at the present time.

abstract: (Member of Council): There is one point in connection with the remarks made by Mr. Kirkland at the last meeting to which I would like to refer. He mentions oil being shipped in packages that may absorb dirt. This I do not think is usual. The oil, as a rule, arrives here clean. It was not dirt that I was referring to in my remarks previously, but moisture. Mr. Kirkland tells us, further, that filter paper will remove all water from the oil, as well as dirt. I do not agree with Mr. Kirkland. It will remove the dirt undoubtedly; but I should certainly dry the oil and not trust to the blotting paper for removing all the water. Prof. Buchanan asks how to get rid of the water. This can best be done by heating the oil to a temperature above the boiling point of water; this will evaporate all water, but not the oil, as its boiling point is considerably higher.

abstract: (Associate): There is little in the author's paper that lends itself to discussion or criticism, the paper being chiefly a description of the Marconi system as installed at the Bluff, Durban. I had the pleasure recently of visiting, the station at Slangkop, Capetown, which is a more up-to-date and more powerful station than that at Durban. There is one improvement in particular which may be of interest to members, that is the use of the rotary spark gap. This is now, I understand, used in all the new Marconi stations, and a short description of it will not, I think, be out of place here.

articleTitle: The troubles of cables
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: (Member of Council) : I have been gratified at the amount of discussion raised by my paper, also at the way members have given their experience with cables, and wish to thank all members who have taken part. There are two points in Mr. Wilson's paper which I wish to deal with. First, in comparing the question of faults on V.B. and L.C. cables he admits that with the L.C. cables a shut down of, at any rate, a small section is inevitable, and he must not forget that this fault has to be located and isolated before supply can be resumed, whereas with V.B. cables the fault can be located and often repaired without any shut down at all. Second, in my remarks on joint boxes I mention that with stuffing gland boxes there should be an opening from the box to the stuffing gland. This, I fear, was not very clearly explained as Mr. Wilson has evidently misunderstood me. The cable is fixed and rigidly held by the stuffing gland partition, and the slot between the two halves of the partition, which is about a quarter of an inch wide, is sufficient to allow the compound to run through when filling the box.

abstract: The President : Those of you who have read Mr. McCann's paper will notice that he confines his remarks to two-stage compressors, either large compressors direct coupled to steam engines, large compressors belt driven by motors, or small compressors belt or gear driven. Apparently he is considering only those types of compressors which up till recently have been general on the Rand. As you know, there are now some very large compressors here of the turbine type being put in both at Rosherville and at the Robinson Mine, and if any gentleman present has anything he can tell us about that type of compressor, as compared with reciprocating compressors, I am sure it would be a valuable contribution.

articleTitle: Electrical separators
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: (Hon. Treasurer) : In a country like this, with propositions so widely distributed and so isolated, I think this subject, which Mr. Woodworth has brought up so ably, is one deserving of discussion by every member. I hope before the discussion closes to have something more to say about it myself, but in the meantime, I should like to ask the author if he would kindly give us in his reply some information relating to the class 5 machines — separators using static electricity. He refers to the fact that in the United States and Mexico particularly, such machines are very largely used, and are very successful. Many of you know that Professor Dobson, some time ago, carried out a number of experiments with a static separator in the laboratory of this College, but I do not know that any practical result came from them. At any rate, many points were brought forward which were of great interest. Personally, I know very little about these static separators and bow far they have been successful in other parts of the world, but 1 am sure that if Mr. Woodworth would give us some figures in connection with them, they would be much appreciated. The static machine, which was used in connection with the experiments I have mentioned, is in the laboratory now, and members will have an opportunity of seeing it working at the close of this meeting.

articleTitle: The design and installation of transformers from an operating point of view
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: (Member of Council) : “We were told by Mr. Kirkland at a previous meeting that the manufacturer lives with the transformers in a way the user does not. At our last meeting Mr. Michell gave us an excellent example of how the manufacturer lives with the transformer. He told us he went through various factories and saw various apparatus in course of manufacture, the various processes being carried out by men, women and girls, who know little of, and trouble, less about the ultimate unit. This is the usual practice as I think Mr. Kirkland will admit, and also that after the preliminary experimental work on any new design that the processes of manufacture and test of apparatus becomes more or less automatic. The man who really lives with transformers, is the engineer responsible for maintaining and receiving the transmission and distribution systems of Power Companies.

abstract: (Member) : The main object of both papers about electric winders submitted for discussion is to show the superiority of the electric winder over the steam winder from the economic point of view. It will be noticed that at the commencement of the discussion the above mentioned point of view has not received that interest the authors expected. It appeared to me that a comparison of cost at hand of actual figures between the two winding systems adopted on the Rand would have created more interest. The available data do not permit of any com parison for reasons I have exhaustively explained in a previous paper.

articleTitle: Notes on some modern electrical machinery
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: During a recent trip to Europe the writer visited several electrical factories and works, and in response to an invitation from the Council of this Institute presents the following notes, dealing briefly with some of the modern machinery inspected. The following important factories and works were visited :— Siemens’ Dynamo Works, Stafford: Siemens’ Cable Works, Woolwich; A.E.G. Turbo-Generator Works, Berlin; A.E.G. Dynamo Works, Berlin; Siemens’ Dynamo Works, Berlin; Siemens’ Cable Works, Berlin; Greenwich Power Station; Moabit Power Station, Berlin. In addition to the above, other large power plants were visited, at one of which the engineer, in order to save copper, has eliminated the negative bus-bar, joining the negative leads together at a convenient point. During a cycle tour some interesting small hydro-electric plants were discovered, one of which, at Porlock in Somerset, consists simply of a bucket water wheel driving a dynamo.

abstract: The Chairman: I was not aware of the fact that Mr. Askew's paper— “ Practical Operation of Three-Phase Hoists at the Bantjes Consolidated Mines, Limited,” was taken together with Mr. Ewing's for the purpose of discussion. I had not the pleasure of being at the meeting, as I was out of town at the time, but I read Mr. Ewing's paper, and found it very interesting, as was also the discussion that followed, with regard to the actual hoisting conditions as they were at the Brakpan Mines. There, as you will recall, the interesting fact exists that there is a large three-phase winder with directly coupled motor operating in the same engine room with a large Ward-Leonard hoist. Mr. Ewing gave some practical comparisons of the operation of these two hoists, but I think that he did not give us the benefit of his experience in connection with the relative operating costs and fuel consumption of the two types of hoists. I hope that Mr. Ewing will be able to give us later the benefit of further experience of the two types of hoists, one as compared with the other. It is not entirely necessary that the contributions to this discussion should be directly iu line with the papers themselves. Anybody who has interesting experiences to bring forward in connection with electric hoisting will do us a favour by contributing. It is perfectly certain that some of those present have under their immediate control electric hoists, in connection with which some peculiarly good or bad circumstance has sometimes arisen.

abstract: The discussion on my paper has resulted in little of technical interest. With regard, however, to the point raised by Mr. W. H. Perrow I wish to dispel his impression that the Bluff Station is entirely dependent upon the current supplied to it from the railway generating plant: such is not the case. At the nearest railway station (West's) is provided a stand-by plant consisting of a 6 h.p. petrol engine and generator which, in the event of a break-down in the regular source of supply, can be run up any moment at five minutes’ notice.

articleTitle: Notes of my recent visit home
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: I was so fortunate on my recent trip not only to spend some time in England, but to have a few days in Berlin and a month in America, and during this time I was of course able to imbibe some ideas of recent progress and changes. Among other things which impressed me at home was the tremendously important place in civilisation which has been taken by the wireless telegraph, about which we have just heard some discussion. One does not get out of touch with wireless telegraphy at any point of one's travels. Even on the ship going home there was a Belgian engineer—I think his name was Rosenthal—who had just come from the Congo State where he had been engaged in installing a number of isolated wireless stations.

articleTitle: A comparison of costs between the wardleonard and three-phasewinding systems

abstract: (Member) : In introducing this reply to the discussion on my paper, I find it necessary to emphasise some of my original remarks, because I observe that some of them have been misunderstood. I cannot lay too great stress on the fact that, for the purposes of fair comparison, the two systems were considered with reference to a modern well-equipped winding installation, shaft and underground arrangements working under economical conditions, such as, in my opinion, may reasonably be considered attainable. In my reply to Mr. Ewing's contribution to the discussion, I have endeavoured to shew how, in the far simpler case of the cylindrical drum tail rope winders cited by him, departures from the assumed economical conditions affect the situation.

articleTitle: A few examples of electrically-operated mechanical appliances
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: In the first instance I am dealing with R. Waygood ∧ Co.'s electrically-operated passenger lift. The large diagram, which is reproduced, shows the electrical equipment and connections for a dual control lift—that is, a lift that can be operated either by a pilot in the car, or by throwing over a switch can be operated from the floors or from the car by push buttons. The motor is 12 h.p. D.C. shunt wound, and runs at either 755 or 410 revolutions per minute ; the driving is effected by a winding drum, this method being used on account of there being no slip, and so the positive automatic cut-off can be adjusted to stop the cage at the various floors without any difficulty.

abstract: (Member of Council): Seeing the great interest which is being aroused by the discussion, I might with advantage give a few more particulars of operating transformers. It is rather an unpleasant experience to look back upon (it was in December, 1908), relating to the breakdown of some, transformers in a terminal sub-station. There were six transformers installed, three J.00 K.V.A., three 50 K.V.A. single-phase (numbered 1, 2,3 and 4, 5, 6 respectively) and over a period of seven months four of them broke down. The order of their breaking down was as follows :—Nos. 1, 2, 6, 1. These breakdowns were no doubt due entirely to the surges of the system, which had full force and effect at this terminal sub-station. Since this sub-station has been linked, or rung up, with others and electrolytic arresters fitted, I have not heard of similar trouble.

articleTitle: Atmospheric phenomena & their relation to the production of over-voltages in overhead electric transmission lines
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: In replying to the discussion on my paper, I shall deal with them in the order in which they occurred In reply to the contribution of Mr. Kirkland I must first thank him for some illuminating remarks on lightning phenomena, although it seems that he is speaking from the American standpoint rather than that of local conditions. He makes two statements to which I must take exception, firstly, the capacity of a sphere is proportional to its radius and not to the square of its radius as he states, and secondly, I cannot agree with him that a lightning- flash one mile in length, is unheard of. He assumes that most discharges occur as an equalisation of potential from point to point in a cloud and not as in the case of a condenser bursting its dielectric. This seems to be the general opinion with American authorities, and I have no doubt he is quoting largely from their views. For instance, in a paper read before the N.E.L.A., June, 1907, by Dr. C. P. Steinmetz, I find the following statement: “Lightning flashes usually occur within thunder clouds and only rarely from cloud to cloud or from cloud to ground. This seems to sum up American opinion on the subject, but I do not agree with it—not for conditions existing in south Africa, at any rate.
